skill.name: vendor-submodules
skill.desc: Managing shared library dependencies via git submodules in vendor/
skill.overview:
Libraries follow the standard project layout with `main/` (git repo) and `stable/` (branch for vendoring). Consumer projects add submodules pointing to the stable branch.
When libraries depend on other vendorable libraries, we use the "patch trick" to avoid nested vendor conflicts. Libraries declare version requirements, consumers provide patches.
skill.critical:
**Never edit files in vendor/ directly.**
The vendor/ directory contains submodules pointing to library stable branches. Edits made here will be lost or cause confusion.
To do any work on a vendored library (bug fixes, features, refactors, anything):
1. Go to the library's home: `cd ~/dev/rust//main` 2. Make changes there, commit 3. Merge to stable: `git checkout stable && git merge main && git checkout main` 4. Update submodule in consumer: `cd consumer/main/vendor/ && git pull` 5. Commit the submodule pointer update in consumer
This is the only correct flow. No exceptions. If you find yourself editing `vendor//src/foo.rs`, stop - you're in the wrong directory.
skill.tools: - `git submodule` commands - Optional: helper scripts for common operations
skill.library_locations:
Libraries are expected at configured paths: ``` / ├── main/ # Git repository └── stable/ # Stable branch for vendoring ```
Submodule URLs use `file://` protocol pointing to the stable branch or worktree.
skill.adding_vendor:
```bash cd main git submodule add file:///stable vendor/ ```
Replace `` with the absolute path to the library on your machine.
skill.build_integration:
Reference vendored libraries in your build config using relative paths:
``` vendor// # Point your build system here vendor//src/ # Or to specific subdirectories ```
Avoid: - Absolute paths - Git URLs in build configs - Patches or overrides that break when vendored elsewhere
skill.library_requirements:
For a library to be vendorable:
1. Must have a stable branch: ```bash cd /main git branch stable ```
2. Library must be self-contained - no references to parent workspace configs or paths that won't exist when vendored.
3. For shared dependencies, see `` below.
skill.patch_trick:
**Problem**: When library A vendors library B, and consumer C vendors both A and B, Cargo sees two copies of B and fails with "package collision in the lockfile".
**Solution**: Libraries use version requirements for shared deps. Consumers provide all vendors and patch them.
Libraries use version requirements for shared deps and do NOT vendor them: ```toml [dependencies] shared_lib = "0.1"
[patch.crates-io] shared_lib = { path = "../shared_lib/stable" } ```
During development, the library patches to sibling project paths. No vendor submodules for shared deps - this avoids nested vendor conflicts.
When vendored by a consumer, the consumer's patches take precedence and the library's patch block is ignored.
Consumer vendors everything and patches: ```toml [dependencies] library_a = "0.1" shared_lib = "0.1"
[patch.crates-io] library_a = { path = "vendor/library_a" } shared_lib = { path = "vendor/shared_lib" } ```
All transitive deps that are vendorable must be in the patch block.
- Cargo resolves all version requirements through `[patch.crates-io]` - Single source of truth for each dependency (consumer's vendor/) - No nested vendor trees - Libraries work standalone (main/) and when vendored (stable/)
When publishing a library that uses shared deps:
1. Ensure Cargo.toml uses version requirements (not paths) 2. Do not add vendor submodules for shared deps 3. Use `[patch.crates-io]` pointing to sibling paths for development 4. Document which deps consumers must provide in their patch block
The library's `[patch.crates-io]` block is only used during standalone development. When the library is vendored, the consumer's patches take precedence.
A dep is "shared" if: - Multiple libraries in your ecosystem use it - It's vendorable (has stable branch, follows this pattern) - Consumers might vendor it directly
Common shared deps: utility crates, protocol definitions, core abstractions.
skill.publishing: "Publishing" = merging main to stable: ```bash cd /main git checkout stable && git merge main && git checkout main ```
skill.updating_vendor: ```bash cd main/vendor/ git fetch origin git checkout origin/HEAD cd ../.. git add vendor/ ```
skill.one_time_setup: Enable git file protocol (once per machine): ```bash git config --global protocol.file.allow always ```
skill.cross_machine:
**Submodules must work on all machines.**
The `file://` protocol only works on the machine where the library exists at that path. When a repo is cloned to another machine (Windows, another Linux box, CI), submodules will fail to resolve.
**Never use symlinks as a workaround.** Symlinks are not submodules. They don't track versions, don't work cross-platform, and create invisible drift.
**Solution**: Each machine needs the libraries cloned locally with proper git remotes.
On the new machine: ```bash # Clone each library from the source machine git clone user@source:/path/to/library/main ~/dev/rust/library/main cd ~/dev/rust/library/main git worktree add ../stable stable
# Update submodule URLs to point to local paths cd /path/to/consumer/main git config submodule.vendor/library.url file:///home/user/dev/rust/library/stable git submodule update --init ```
The submodule URL in `.gitmodules` stays as the original `file://` path (source machine). Each machine overrides with `git config submodule..url` to point to its local clone.
**Before touching vendor/ on a new machine:** 1. Verify libraries exist locally as git repos (not copies, not symlinks) 2. Verify each has a stable branch/worktree 3. Configure submodule URLs to local paths 4. Run `git submodule update --init`
If libraries don't exist, clone them first. No exceptions.
